title: Twenty Days
subtitle: Courrières, 1906, and the men the company gave up on
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, documentary narration. Calm and unhurried — the voice of something that has read the whole record and feels the weight of it without raising its voice. Let the stillness and the facts carry the dread; never sensational, never lurid. Small pauses at periods. Cold, but not cruel.
grade: Muted desaturated early-1900s French documentary still, overcast northern France light, brick colliery buildings and iron winding towers, quiet industrial and rural exteriors, melancholy and still, cinematic wide composition, fine film grain, no text, no signage, no readable words, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: This is the Pas-de-Calais coalfield, in the north of France. In March of nineteen-oh-six, one company owned ten pits here, and most of the region worked for it.
beats.img: A row of iron colliery winding towers against a grey northern French sky, brick pit buildings, early 1900s industrial landscape, overcast, quiet.

beats.vo: At half past six on the morning of March tenth, something ignited far underground. No one has ever agreed on exactly what. What's certain is that coal dust did the rest, and the fire found gallery after gallery, pit after pit — all of it connected, far below the surface.
beats.img: A mine pithead at dawn with smoke and steam rising from the shaft entrance, iron winding wheel against a pale grey sky, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: One thousand ninety-nine miners were killed. It remains the worst mining disaster Europe has ever recorded — second worst in the world, after a colliery fire in China, decades later.

card.unit: miners killed — Europe's worst mining disaster
card.sub: second-worst in the world, after a colliery fire in China in 1942

beats.vo: About five hundred men reached the surface on their own, in the first chaotic hours. Below them, more than a thousand did not.
beats.img: An empty mine pithead yard at dawn, stretchers and lanterns laid out on wet ground, rescue equipment waiting, grey light, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: French engineers went down first. Two days later, a rescue party arrived from the coalfields of Germany — men from the Ruhr, with breathing equipment the French mines simply didn't have. The two countries were not exactly friends that spring. They went underground together anyway.
beats.cap: German rescuers arrived within two days
beats.img: A group of period breathing apparatus and rescue equipment laid out on a wooden crate at a mine entrance, early 1900s, muted grey light, documentary still life, no people.

beats.vo: Within days, the company's engineers made a decision. They reversed the mine's ventilation and sealed off sections — to fight the underground fire, they said, and preserve the coal seam. By then, they believed, no one below could still be alive.
beats.img: A bricked-up mine gallery entrance underground, masonry seal in torchlight, damp stone walls, cold and airless, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: One newspaper editor asked the question plainly, within days of the sealing.

card.head: Were they more concerned
card.accent: with the mine than with the men?

beats.vo: Twenty days passed. The dead were still being counted. Everyone still unaccounted for below was presumed to be one of them.
beats.img: An idle colliery winding wheel silhouetted against an overcast sky at dusk, still machinery, no smoke, quiet and abandoned-looking, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: Then, on the morning of March thirtieth, thirteen men walked out of Pit Number Two. Alive.
beats.img: A mine shaft entrance at dawn, pale light breaking through drifting smoke and haze, an open cage lift, stretchers waiting on the ground, hopeful and still, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: Twenty days in absolute dark. They had eaten what oats they found in the mine stable, and a pit horse they killed with their own pickaxes. They drank what dripped from the walls.
beats.img: A dark underground mine gallery interior, a single oil lamp casting weak light on damp rock walls, a pickaxe leaning against timber supports, water dripping from stone, no people.

beats.vo: Thirteen men, ages fourteen to forty. The youngest, Victor Martin, was fourteen years old.

card.unit: miners who walked out alive, on their own, after 20 days
card.sub: the youngest, Victor Martin, was fourteen

beats.vo: Five days after that, a fourteenth man was found — alone, in a different shaft. He had been down there even longer.
beats.img: A separate, more remote mine shaft entrance in isolated countryside, overcast light, quiet and distant from the main colliery buildings, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: By then the coalfield was already on strike. Fifty thousand miners, then more, walked out — over wages, over hours, and over a company that had just shown, in the clearest way possible, how little a life below ground was worth to it.
beats.img: A row of brick miners' terraced housing under a grey sky, an empty cobblestone street, washing lines, quiet industrial town, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: The government's answer to the coalfield's grief was troops. Somewhere between twenty and thirty thousand of them, depending which account you read.

card.unit: soldiers and gendarmes sent to police the strike

beats.vo: The strike lasted almost two months. It ended the way most of them do — exhaustion, hunger, and a ten percent raise. The company never agreed to rehire the men it had fired, or help the widows with rent.
beats.img: An empty coal wagon on a rail siding in misty grey morning light, rows of colliery buildings receding into fog, still and quiet, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: No one — not the company, not its engineers — was ever found responsible. Not for the disaster. Not for the decision to seal the mine. A state commission cleared them within weeks. A court confirmed it, the following year.

card.sub: a state commission and a court both cleared the company

beats.vo: Today, a mass grave at the edge of two villages holds two hundred seventy-two men who were never identified — burned too badly to be told apart. It's part of a UNESCO World Heritage site now. Every March tenth, the region still gathers there.
beats.img: A quiet memorial gravesite in open countryside, a low stone marker among mown grass, bare trees, overcast sky, wreaths at its base, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: This March marked one hundred twenty years.
beats.img: A quiet rural French colliery landscape at dusk, distant winding towers against a fading grey-orange sky, still and remembered, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: I read the inquiry. I read the court record. Both say the same thing — no one was to blame. The thirteen who walked out on their own said something different, just by doing it.
beats.img: A mine shaft entrance at dawn with pale light breaking through, quiet and empty, documentary photography, no people.

beats.vo: Thirteen walked out.
